camille: FYI — after last night's canary we saw a ~12% host CPU uplift for 8k/seq requests. Top stack on the flame is host-tokenize -> grpc::Writev -> small memcpy loops. attaching quick perf sample below.

raj: ugh. small writes over grpc are the usual suspect. do we have an increase in micro-batches or more prefix-only requests?

camille: Perf sample (very shortened):
```
  samples: 1200
  30.4%  host_proc  [.] HostTokenizer::tokenize
  22.1%  host_proc  [.] grpc::Writev
  12.7%  host_proc  [.] KVCache::fetch_if_hot
  8.5%   host_proc  [.] memcpy
```
Stack trace shows many tiny allocations and repeated writev syscalls (~20k/s).

marta: KV hits look stable overall but hot-shard misses spiked during canary bursts — could be batch boundary alignment moving previously-cached prefixes out of cache.

oliver: Two levers to try: coalesce writev on the host side (merge small fragments before sending) and bias batching heuristic to prefer slightly larger batches when KV hit probability is high. also consider reserving an arena for token buffers to avoid repeated allocs.

raj: I can prototype a writev coalesce in the Rust shim this morning. naive patch: accumulate outgoing iovecs up to 64KB or N entries, then do one writev. pseudo: 
```
let mut iov = Vec::new();
for frag in outgoing { iov.push(frag); if iov.len() >= 64 || total_bytes(iov) >= 64*1024 { send_writev(&iov); iov.clear(); } }
if !iov.is_empty() { send_writev(&iov) }
```
Might reduce syscall pressure but could add latency for very low-rate streams.

camille: agree. we should gate by window + max-latency. we saw tail requests require sub-10ms end-to-end for some routes, so coalescing mustn't add >2ms on 99th. propose experiment matrix:
- A: writev coalesce with 1ms flush window
- B: writev coalesce with 3ms flush window + kv-priority batching (prefer to flush when cache hit score >= 0.7)
- C: fallback only on >1 fragment per request (safe opt-in)

marta: I'll pull kv hot-shard traces and compute a per-request cache-probability metric we can expose to the router to make that batching decision. should have numbers in ~2 hours.

raj: implementing A and C now. will add a config flag and perf traces.

infra-bot: deploy queued: canary/host-shim-writev-coalesce -> env:staging at 7765432118 (automated) :package:

oliver: Also double-check kernel knobs: TCP small-queue settings + GRO/GSO behaviour can affect how many syscalls actually hit the wire. on our VMs, `net.ipv4.tcp_mtu_probing` and `tcp_max_syn_backlog` were tuned previously — ping infra to ensure settings match dedicated hosts.

camille: Good call. raj, please include a run of `ss -tin` and `perf record -g` for the canary, and dump a flamegraph. marta, once you have cache probability we can try B.

raj: will post perf + flamegraph by ~7765432124.

marta: KV metric posted: sample route has hit-prob ~0.82 for lengths >512 tokens in non-streaming flows. streaming short prefixes are the ones that tank the cache.

camille: Perfect. Plan: roll A first with 1ms window, measure cpu and p99 latency, then B if CPU stays high. if p99 regresses >1.5x revert. tagging @raj and @marta to own experiments. :rocket:

oliver: If we still see memcpy hotspots after coalescing, we should look at buffer layout: interleaved token structs -> flatten to single contiguous bytes to make memcpy larger but fewer ops.

camille: Thanks — keeping this thread for results. short updates only please. :thumbsup:
